paper_a.title: The Primes Contain Arbitrarily Long Arithmetic Progressions (Green & Tao, 2004)

paper_b.title: On Sets of Integers Containing No k Elements in Arithmetic Progression (Szemeredi, 1975)

metadata.description: Green-Tao extends Szemeredi's theorem from subsets of integers with positive density to the primes (which have density zero). The extension is achieved via a transference principle: embed the primes in a pseudorandom set where they have positive relative density, then transfer Szemeredi's theorem to work for dense subsets of pseudorandom sets. Szemeredi's theorem is used as a black-box ingredient.

matches.explanation: Both prove existence of arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions, but for different sets. Szemeredi: any subset of $[N]$ with $|A| \geq \delta N$ (positive density). Green-Tao: the primes (density zero, $\pi(N) \sim N/\log N$). Green-Tao is a strict generalization in the sense that the primes are a set where Szemeredi's theorem does not directly apply.

Green-Tao uses Szemeredi's theorem as a literal black-box input. The statement they invoke is identical: dense subsets of $[N]$ contain long APs. This is one of the three main ingredients of the Green-Tao proof.
Both define arithmetic progressions identically. Green-Tao restricts to APs in the primes; Szemeredi considers APs in arbitrary dense subsets.

Green-Tao explicitly discusses why positive density is needed for Szemeredi's theorem and why the primes (density zero) require a new idea. The solution: relative density in a pseudorandom set replaces absolute density.

The relative Szemeredi theorem (transference principle) is the main new contribution of Green-Tao. It states that any set with positive relative density in a pseudorandom measure contains long APs. This has no counterpart in Szemeredi, who works in the absolute density setting.

The concept of a pseudorandom measure (satisfying linear forms and correlation conditions) is entirely new in Green-Tao. Szemeredi's proof uses regularity/density-increment machinery, not pseudorandomness.

The Goldston-Yildirim sieve construction of a pseudorandom majorant for the primes is specific to Green-Tao's number-theoretic setting. It provides the bridge between sieve theory and additive combinatorics.
The W-trick (working in residue classes to remove small-prime biases) is a technical device specific to Green-Tao's number-theoretic context.

Both proofs are highly complex but use fundamentally different techniques. Szemeredi: regularity lemma + counting lemma + density increment (purely combinatorial). Green-Tao: transference principle + pseudorandom majorant + Szemeredi as black box. Green-Tao's proof structure is a paradigm shift: it reduces the number-theoretic problem to Szemeredi plus sieve theory.

Both discuss quantitative bounds. Szemeredi's bounds are tower-type. Green-Tao inherits these tower-type bounds (through their use of Szemeredi's theorem) and adds additional losses from the sieve and transference. Both papers note the bounds are far from conjectured truth.
